Use the interval basis of the order topologies and prove the two conjuncts separately by a local squeezing argument.

- Strictly monotone case: Given a basic neighborhood of \(f(a)\), use that \(f(s)\) is also a neighborhood and that \(\beta\) is densely ordered to choose values of \(f(s)\) inside the target neighborhood, on each relevant side of \(f(a)\). Choose preimages \(x,y\in s\). Strict monotonicity forces \(x<a<y\), and for
  \[
  z\in s\cap (x,y)
  \]
  it gives \(f(x)<f(z)<f(y)\). Thus a neighborhood of \(a\) is mapped into the prescribed neighborhood of \(f(a)\). Endpoint cases use the corresponding one-sided rays.

- Monotone one-sided case: Work with basic relative neighborhoods \((c,f(a)]\subseteq Iic(f(a))\). From
  \(f(s)\in\mathcal N[Iic(f(a))](f(a))\), choose \(b\in f(s)\) with
  \(c<b<f(a)\), and write \(b=f(x)\) for \(x\in s\). Since
  \(s\in\mathcal N[Iic(a)](a)\), in particular \(a\in s\); monotonicity then forces \(x<a\). For \(z\in s\cap(x,a]\),
  \[
  b=f(x)\le f(z)\le f(a),
  \]
  so the relative neighborhood \(s\cap(x,a]\) maps into \((c,f(a)]\).

The essential role of dense order is to provide anchor values strictly between the boundary of a target interval and \(f(a)\); strict monotonicity in the first conjunct then converts their position in the codomain into the required ordering of their preimages.
